query: Which hierarchical estimation strategies (partial pooling, informative priors, adaptive stopping) most reduce ambulatory trial burden while preserving identifiability of within-person effort dynamics?

response.query: Which hierarchical estimation strategies (partial pooling, informative priors, adaptive stopping) most reduce ambulatory trial burden while preserving identifiability of within-person effort dynamics?
response.answer: Informative priors and adaptive stopping most reduce trial burden while preserving identifiability. Hierarchical estimation strategies like partial pooling also help.

results.title: Efficient Diffusion-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation with Hierarchical Temporal Pruning
results.content: In this paper, we propose an Efficient Diffusion-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation framework with a Hierarchical Temporal Pruning (HTP) strategy, which dynamically prunes redundant pose tokens across both frame and semantic levels while preserving critical motion dynamics. HTP operates in a staged, top-down manner: (1) Temporal Correlation-Enhanced Pruning (TCEP) identifies essential frames by analyzing inter-frame motion correlations through adaptive temporal graph construction; (2) Sparse-Focused Temporal MHSA (SFT MHSA) leverages the resulting frame-level sparsity to reduce attention computation, focusing on motion-relevant tokens; and (3) Mask-Guided Pose Token Pruner (MGPTP) performs fine-grained semantic pruning via clustering, retaining only the most informative pose tokens. To address these challenges, we propose an efficient diffusion-based 3D human pose estimation framework with Hierarchical Temporal Pruning (HTP), which operates across both frame-level and semantic-level stages to preserve essential motion dynamics throughout the denoising process. As shown in Fig. 4 ‣ IV Method ‣ Efficient Diffusion-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation with Hierarchical Temporal Pruning"), given the pose tokens after SFT MHSA, , we apply average pooling along the joint dimension to obtain frame-wise tokens .

results.title: Hierarchical modeling when you have only 2 groups:  I still think it’s a good idea, you just need an informative prior on the group-level variation | Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science
results.content: # Hierarchical modeling when you have only 2 groups: I still think it’s a good idea, you just need an informative prior on the group-level variation. My quick answer is that I do think a hierarchical model is appropriate here, but, with data on only 2 groups, it will be necessary to put strong prior information on the between-groups sd parameter tau. If you simply put the default uniform prior on that group-level scale parameter, all the posterior mass will be at tau = infinity, and you’ll do no pooling at all. Anyway, the benefit of the hierarchical model is that it gives you partial pooling and thus more efficient estimates of the parameters in each group. You just need to supply some prior information on how different the groups might be. Now, at this point, you (or maybe not you, but someone else) might want to be a “tough guy” and say you want to be entirely data-based, you don’t want to do any partial pooling here, maybe you’re ok with hierarchical models with hyperparameters estimated from data but to put in strong prior information to enforce partial pooling, that’s a step too far. Hence you’ll end up aggregating your data in some way—across drugs, or across disparate groups of patients, or over time—in order to have enough of a sample size for the no-pooling approach to work. Before, I was essentially using an informative prior to determine pooling by using a weighted version of the earlier study to define the prior for my single-level model. Since my informative prior is going to dictate the amount of pooling, would you find it useful to report the results with different priors? ## 3 thoughts on “Hierarchical modeling when you have only 2 groups: I still think it’s a good idea, you just need an informative prior on the group-level variation”. 1. “Hence you’ll end up aggregating your data in some way—across drugs, or across disparate groups of patients, or over time—in order to have enough of a sample size for the no-pooling approach to work.”. With only 2 groups, you need strong prior information on the between-group variance.

results.title: [2507.20288] A nonparametric approach to practical identifiability of nonlinear mixed effects models
results.content: Submitted on 27 Jul 2025 ([v1), last revised 17 Nov 2025 (this version, v2)]. # Title:A nonparametric approach to practical identifiability of nonlinear mixed effects models. View a PDF of the paper titled A nonparametric approach to practical identifiability of nonlinear mixed effects models, by Tyler Cassidy and 6 other authors. > Abstract:Mathematical modelling is a widely used approach to understand and interpret clinical trial data. This modelling typically involves fitting mechanistic mathematical models to data from individual trial participants. Despite the widespread adoption of this individual-based fitting, it is becoming increasingly common to take a hierarchical approach to parameter estimation, where modellers characterize the population parameter distributions, rather than considering each individual independently. This hierarchical parameter estimation is standard in pharmacometric modelling. However, many of the existing techniques for parameter identifiability do not immediately translate from the individual-based fitting to the hierarchical setting. Here, we propose a nonparametric approach to study practical identifiability within a hierarchical parameter estimation framework. We focus on the commonly used nonlinear mixed effects framework and investigate two well-studied examples from the pharmacometrics and viral dynamics literature to illustrate the potential utility of our approach. **** Sun, 27 Jul 2025 14:07:09 UTC (5,921 KB). **[v2]** Mon, 17 Nov 2025 10:27:25 UTC (7,794 KB). ## Access Paper:. results.title: Effects of sceptical priors on the performance of adaptive clinical trials with binary outcomes. - Granholm - 2024 - Pharmaceutical Statistics - Wiley Online Library
results.content: As such, the ‘best’ prior may depend on the relative importance of economical/logistical considerations (total sample sizes), benefits to patients *internal* to the trial (total event counts/rates), benefits to patients *external* to the trial (probability of conclusiveness/superiority/selecting of the best arm and IDP), or statistical accuracy (RMSEs).2, 4, 13 At any rate, a prior conveying *some* information may be more appropriate than priors with relatively high probabilities of improbable effect sizes27 and will usually facilitate and speed up realistic analyses with complex models that require, for example, Markov chain Monte Carlo-methods instead of conjugate analysis.20, 28 To explain and justify the use of neutral sceptical priors to trial team members and readers, ‘translating’ the amount of information provided by the prior to a clinically interpretable scale (e.g., the corresponding number of participants in a two-arm trial with identical outcomes in both arms) may be helpful.6, 15 Similarly, comparisons with conventional group-sequential designs may ease explanation, as the effects of using non-informative and strongly sceptical neutral priors on the performance of adaptive designs with constant stopping rules may resemble the use of Pocock and O'Brien-Fleming monitoring boundaries, respectively.16, 29. First, it was conducted according to a publicly available protocol and statistical analysis plan,11 which prevents selective reporting and cherry-picking of interesting results, even for simulation studies, in which random error is not of concern due to the large number of simulations conducted.2, 3 Second, while we planned to use only the same, fixed stopping thresholds for all simulations,11 we supplemented this with analyses using stopping thresholds calibrated to control the type 1 error rates at approximately 5%, as has been done in other studies.4, 13, 14 Presenting both sets of analyses provides additional valuable insights, and while the pre-planned analyses simultaneously (yet, independently) assessed the influence on all metrics (including type 1 and 2 error rates), this may not resemble a realistic clinical trial design phase, in which equivalent type 1 error rates for all design/prior combinations may be preferred, as controlling the type 1 error at an acceptable level will generally be required by regulatory agencies.18 Third, while it is impossible to cover every possible scenario or design choice, we covered a substantial proportion of trial designs under three sensible effect-size scenarios and six carefully chosen priors.
